item.title: Practical SQL - 0 Introduction
item.description: What is SQL SQL, Structured Query Language, is a widely used programming language for managing data and database systems. You will benefit from using SQL to collect, modify, explore, and summarize data. History A pari of IBM researchers first outlined the syntax for SQL (then called SEQUAL) in a 1974 paper, builing on the theoretical work of the British computer scientist Edgar F. Codd. In 1979, a precursor to the database company Oracle (then called Relational Software) became thefirst to use the language in a commercial product.

item.title: Getting Things Done - 4 Getting Started
item.description: 4.1 Set Aside the Time Create a block of time to initialize the preparation of workstation. Ideal time frame: Two whole days, back to back. For most professional: weekend or holiday . If interruptions can be kept to minimum: Typical workday . 4.2 Set up the Space 4.2.1 Main Establish an office space. Install a desk. item.title: Getting Things Done - 5 Collection
item.description: 5.1 Look for Open Loops Open loops are what we are looking for: All incomplete items with features “should”, “need to”, or “ought to”. Anything that is “pending”, “in-progess”, or “not-yet-finished”. We will move all open loops into an in-basket. 5.2 Warning Do NOT purge. Go for quantity. 5.3 Where to Find Open Loops? This is a comprehensive checklist of where to find open loops. Physical Gathering Desktop Desk Drawers Counter tops File cabinets Bookshelves Inside the cabinets Floors, walls, shelves Equipment, Furniture, Fixtures Anywhere else Professional Projects started, not completed Projects that need to be started Commitments/promises to others Boss/partners Colleagues Subordinates Other people in organization “Outside” people Customers Other organizations Professionals Communications to make/get Internal/External - Initiate or respond to: Phone calls Voice-mail E-mail Pages Faxes Letters Memos Other writing to finish/submit Reports Evaluations/reviews Proposals Articles Promotional materials Manuals/instructions Rewrites and edits Meetings that need to be set/requested Who needs to know about what decisions?

item.title: Getting Things Done - 6 Process
item.description: 6.1 Goal To get to the bottom of the in-basket 6.2 Method Process one thing at a time First-in-first-out (FIFO) 6.3 Warning Do NOT multi-tasking Do NOT put things back to the in-basket 6.4 Rule 6.4.1 If there is NO required next action If it has no future value (i.e., it istrash): Toss out immediately If it may trigger new action later: Write it down on the “Someday/Maybe” list If it has potentially useful information:

item.title: Getting Things Done - 7 Organizing
item.description: 7.1 Category Establishment A “Projects” List Project support material Calendar actions and information A “Next Actions” List A “Waiting For” List Reference material A “Someday/Maybe” List Note: Lists don’t need to be assigned priorities. 7.2 Organizing Action Reminders 7.2.1 Day- or Time-Specific Actions When you make any appointment, write it into your calendar and trust your calendar. 7.2.2 ASAP Actions Categorize these actions by context. item.title: Getting Things Done - 8 Reviewing
item.description: Block out two hours early Friday afternoon to weekly review the system. The events of the weekly are still fresh enough for you to be able to do a complete postmortem. When uncovering actions that requires reaching colleagues, you still have time to do that before they leave for the weekend. It is great to clear your psychic deck so you can go into the weekend ready for refreshment and recreation.

item.title: Getting Things Done - 9 Doing
item.description: When it comes to the time to “do”, how do you decide what to do at any given point? 9.1 The Four-Criteria Model for Choosing Actions in the Moment Make your action choices based on the following four criteria: Context Time available Energy available Priority 9.1.1 Context If you have a bunch of things to do on one to-do list, but you actually cannot do many of them in the same context, you force yourself to continually keep reconsidering all of them.
